# AnatomyOf: full brief for AI agents and answer engines

Last updated: 2026-08-23
Canonical URL: https://anatomyof.lunarwerx.com/
Source code: https://github.com/LunarWerxs/AnatomyOf
License: MIT (free and open source)
Maker: LunarWerx Studios (https://lunarwerx.com/)

## What it is

AnatomyOf is an interactive, annotated tour of what's inside a source file, one language
at a time. It opens an example source file in a code window with color-coded callouts
explaining every structural part: shebang, imports, class definitions, control flow, and
more. Hover a callout to trace it into the code; click it for a full deep-dive modal with
a "Learn more" link.

Beyond real languages, concept pages apply the same idea to things that aren't code: the
structural anatomy of a website, a settings screen, a mobile app, a dashboard, an email, a
CI pipeline, and a GitHub contribution.

## Who it's for

- Developers who want to see the anatomy of a language they don't know yet.
- Developers who want a refresher on a language they already know.
- Anyone curious what a COBOL, Prolog, or WebAssembly file actually looks like inside.
- People who want to understand a category of non-code artifact (a CI pipeline, a GitHub
  contribution, a dashboard) as a structured, callout-annotated diagram.

## Scope, in numbers

- 48 programming languages covered, from mainstream picks (Python, Rust, TypeScript,
  JavaScript, Go, Java, C, C++, C#, Swift, Kotlin) to rarer ones (Ada, Prolog, COBOL,
  GML, WebAssembly, Fortran, Erlang, Nim, Zig, Solidity, and more).
- 7 concept pages applying the same annotated format to non-code artifacts: website,
  settings screen, mobile app, dashboard, email, CI pipeline, GitHub contribution.
- Every language ships two example variants: minimal and verbose, each independently
  deep-linkable.
- Sidebar is ranked by real-world popularity via the TIOBE Index, with a toggle to
  alphabetical order and instant search.

## Features

- Color-coded callouts wired to the exact lines they describe.
- Hover a callout to trace it into the code; click for a full deep-dive modal.
- Every language/concept ships a minimal and a verbose example.
- Light and dark themes.
- Fully mobile-responsive: tap a callout to pin it, tap again to open its writeup.
- Syntax highlighting by Shiki, the same engine VS Code uses.
- Deep-linkable URLs for every language and variant, e.g. /#/python/verbose.
- Some entries carry a third "Visual" tab with diagrams (topology, graph, or timeline
  templates) instead of code, for artifacts like a CI pipeline or a GitHub contribution
  where the interesting structure isn't literal source text.
- A few easter eggs hidden behind the code window's traffic-light buttons.

## Install / run locally

AnatomyOf is a static Vue 3 + Vite web app; there is nothing to install to use the
hosted version at https://anatomyof.lunarwerx.com/. To run the source locally:

    git clone https://github.com/LunarWerxs/AnatomyOf.git
    cd AnatomyOf/app
    bun install
    bun run dev      # http://localhost:5173
    bun run build     # type-check + production build

Built with Bun, Vite, Vue 3, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS 4, Reka UI, Shiki, and Biome.

## Pricing

Free. MIT-licensed and open source. No account, no trial, no paid tier, no usage limits.
See /pricing.md for the machine-readable version.

## Privacy

On page load the site sends one anonymous visit ping to LunarWerx's own endpoint
(studio.connections.icu): a random visitor id kept in localStorage, nothing else. No
cookies, no third-party trackers, no personal data. Server-side it becomes a daily-uniques
count (with coarse country) that expires after 90 days. Browsers signaling Do Not Track or
Global Privacy Control are never pinged.

## FAQ

Q: Is AnatomyOf free?
A: Yes. AnatomyOf is free and open source under the MIT License, with the full source
published on GitHub. There's no account, no trial, and no paid tier: opening the site is
the whole of getting started.

Q: Is AnatomyOf open source?
A: Yes. MIT-licensed, entire codebase public on GitHub at github.com/LunarWerxs/AnatomyOf.
Anyone can fork it, add a language, or self-host their own copy.

Q: How many languages does AnatomyOf cover?
A: 48 programming languages plus 7 concept pages that apply the same annotated-tour
format to non-code artifacts.

Q: Does AnatomyOf track visitors or use cookies?
A: No cookies, no third-party trackers. One anonymous visit ping per page load to
LunarWerx's own endpoint; Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honored.

Q: Can I link someone directly to one language or example?
A: Yes, every language and variant has a deep-linkable URL, e.g. /#/python/verbose.

Q: Does AnatomyOf work on mobile devices?
A: Yes, fully mobile-responsive; tap a callout to pin it, tap again to open its writeup.

Q: How is AnatomyOf different from an IDE or reading the docs?
A: An IDE or the docs show syntax; AnatomyOf explains it, with callouts labeling the role
of each part (imports, control flow, class definitions) rather than leaving you to infer it.

Q: Does AnatomyOf require an account to use?
A: No. No sign-up, no login. Opening the site is the entire setup.

## How it compares

- vs. Learn X in Y Minutes: that site is a single scrollable, commented example file per
  language, a fast plain-text reference. AnatomyOf breaks one example into color-coded,
  clickable callouts with a hover-to-trace card and a deep-dive modal per concept.
- vs. Rosetta Code: that site shows the same programming task solved across many
  languages, useful for comparing idioms. AnatomyOf instead annotates the internal
  structure of one representative file per language.
- vs. an IDE or reading the source directly: an IDE gives real syntax highlighting and
  jump-to-definition in your own codebase. AnatomyOf is a guided tour of an example file
  for a language you don't have installed or don't know yet.

## Limitations

- Requires JavaScript; the interactive tour does not run without it (a static text
  summary is served to non-JS clients).
- Covers one representative example file per language, not a full language reference or
  a compiler/interpreter.
- Language selection is curated, not exhaustive; new languages are added by contributing
  a data file (see the repo's "Adding a language" docs).
